1:
Everything in the superscription is disputed, beginning with the thirtieth year, which no two voices reckon alike. Gill reports it taken from the last jubilee by several Jewish commentators, or from the finding of the book of the law by Hilkiah, as the Targum paraphrases it; Wesley works that reckoning out, adding fourteen years of Josiah after the law was found to the eleven of the next reign and the five of Jehoiachin. Calvin rejects it as too obscure and forced and unsupported by later writers, and argues for the jubilee as the usual Jewish method and a point of starting for the future, noting that Jerome mentions the opinion although he rejects it. Henry reports two more. Some make it the age of the prophet, who as a priest would then have entered on his office, but being debarred by the calamity of the times was called at that age to the dignity of a prophet instead; Clarke takes this reading. Others reckon from the accession of Nabopolassar, the father of Nebuchadnezzar, from which the Chaldeans began a new computation, that king reigning nineteen years and this being the eleventh of his son. Henry finds it proper enough that a man in Babylon should use the computation used there, as men abroad date by the new style. Ellicott argues from the recurrence of the fifth day in both datings that the two epochs began together.

The setting is filled in from several sides. Keil and Delitzsch give the name as meaning that God strengthens, and place the prophet among the captives taken with the king eleven years before the destruction of the city, living in northern Mesopotamia on the banks of the Chaboras, married and in his own house amid a colony of banished Jews at Tel-abib, called in the fifth year of his banishment. Clarke adds that three thousand of the principal inhabitants went into exile with the king, none being left but the very poorest, and cites an archbishop for the remark that the prophet was present in body among the exiles though in vision sometimes taken to Jerusalem. Wesley thinks the fifth day was probably a sabbath, when the Jews were at leisure to hear him, and that they had retired to the river to lament the desolation of Jerusalem. Ellicott presses a distinction in the word rendered captives: it is the same word used of the king, yet must be understood differently, since he was in prison for many years while his people within certain limits were free, being more than exiles but less than prisoners.

Gill and Ellicott agree that the emphatic form asserts reality, Gill rendering it that the word was in being and Ellicott that it came certainly, the original simply repeating the verb. Ellicott notices that the prophet speaks of himself in the third person here and in the first everywhere afterwards, and names himself only twice, from which it has been suggested that these verses were inserted on a revision of his own work. Calvin asks why the book opens with a conjunction, and answers that an oblique comparison is intended: after God had exercised his servants at Jerusalem, their peculiar seat, to weariness, now at length he speaks in Chaldea. He also dismisses the fancy that the father named was Jeremiah, which rests on nothing but a persuasion that the father of a prophet must himself be one. Clarke and Wesley both read the hand of the Lord as power felt, Wesley adding that it opened the eyes to see, the ear to hear and the heart to receive, and that when the hand goes with the word it becomes effectual. Ellicott closes with a caution for all that follows, that the prophet is struggling to portray what exceeds the power of human language, so that repetition and obscurity in the detail should not surprise us.
4:
Henry and Calvin both begin with what the vision is for. Henry finds three intentions: to fill the prophet with honourable thoughts of the God who commissioned him, so that he may infer it is his honour to serve one whom angels serve, and draws back at his peril, since God can pursue him as he did Jonah; to strike terror into the sinners left in Zion and those already in Babylon, secure and bidding defiance to the threatenings, who must learn that the God they said would leave them in peace is a consuming fire; and to comfort those who trembled at his word. Calvin reduces it to two: God wished first to invest his servant with authority and then to inspire the people with terror, since the prophet laboured among a hard-hearted people whose arrogance had to be subdued, or he spoke to the deaf.

Gill takes the looking as done under the influence of the Spirit, and the midst from which the creatures came as the whole that was seen. The direction of the storm is read two ways. Clarke and Wesley take the north for Babylon, which lay northward of Judea, Clarke naming Nebuchadnezzar and noting that Chaldea is frequently so denominated by Jeremiah, and Wesley that the prophet, though himself in Babylon, speaks of the Jews as if they were in Jerusalem. Ellicott denies any Babylonian notion of a northern seat of divine power, and explains it by prophetic usage, judgments upon Judea being commonly represented as coming from the north because that was the road by which the conquerors descended; the vision is seen in Chaldea but described as if viewed from Jerusalem.

The details of the cloud are worked over closely. Clarke describes a mass of fire concentrated in a vast cloud so that the flames might be more observable, never escaping it but issuing and returning in upon itself, with a fine tinge of light to mark its limits; and he notes that the word we render amber was used of a bright metal of gold and brass. Ellicott renders the infolding fire more literally as catching itself, flames whose flashes succeeded one another so fast that each seemed to lay hold on the one before, and notes that transposing one letter would make the whirlwind bring on the cloud rather than accompany it. He gives the cloud a double office, as the groundwork in which the other details are located and as a hiding place of the divine majesty, so that all may be seen which the eye can bear while what it cannot is still known to be there. Wesley reads the whirlwind as a quick and irresistible vengeance.

What the four creatures are is the largest question. Calvin clears the ground by rejecting four readings: that they are the four seasons, celebrating the government of the world, which he calls far-fetched; that they are four virtues, justice in the man, prudence in the eagle, fortitude in the lion, endurance in the ox, a shrewd conjecture with no solidity; that they are four passions or faculties of the mind, which he calls puerile; and the once received opinion that they are the four Evangelists. His own reading is that they are angels shown under the form of animals, God descending from the sanctuary to appear familiarly on earth, as if to say that he reigns not only among his angels but exercises his power here, his providence being everywhere diffused. Wesley agrees that they are the holy angels, whose being and power derive from God and whose glory is a ray of his. Ellicott holds back from naming them, since the prophet does not here say what they were but recognised them in a later vision as the cherubim; and the word likeness marks them as symbolic and not actually existing creatures, whose one characteristic is that they are living.
6:
How much of each creature there was is disputed first. Calvin reports that many suppose each animal had four heads with four appearances apiece, and others assign four wings to every head or even sixteen; he rejects all of it, since heads and wings correspond and four heads means four wings. Ellicott treats the numbers as of no weight, since the cherubim are variously represented elsewhere with one face or two, and with two wings or six. He allows that more than two suits here, partly as concurring with the other marks of the fulness of their life, partly because two were used to express reverence, which is how Wesley divides them: with two they flew, denoting the speed of their obedience, and with two they covered themselves. Ellicott ranks the four faces, man heading the animal creation, the lion the wild beasts, the ox the domestic, the eagle the birds; Clarke observes that the face of the man was the one presented to the prophet and so seen most plainly, which is why the whole image bore a general resemblance to the human figure; and Gill notes that the Targum multiplies the faces monstrously.

The legs are read for what they exclude. Ellicott renders each leg a straight leg, without bend at the knee, equally fitted for motion in any direction, and the sole not formed like the human foot to move forward only but round and solid. Calvin refers the straightness to the legs as well, so that these creatures stood as men do, since we differ from the brutes that look towards the ground; he quotes a poet on the favour God has conferred on man, that man looks aloft and with erected eyes beholds his own hereditary skies. The roundness he takes for agility: a man who turns right or left feels himself contending with nature if he attempts at the same time to walk backwards, whereas a round foot moves any way easily. Clarke reaches the same conclusion from another quarter, observing that ancient Egyptian images of Isis, Osiris and Anubis show no bend at the knee, and citing the remark of Adrian that the gods are never represented as walking but always gliding, a criterion for telling them from other spirits; Heliodorus gives the same reason for the united feet of the gods. Wesley reads the straightness as strength, a limb bowed to this or that part arguing weakness, and takes the divided hoof for the cleanness of the creature. Both Clarke and Ellicott confine the sparkling to the hoof rather than the whole leg.

The hands under the wings divide them. Clarke doubts whether the arms are not represented as covered with feathers, so that they had the appearance of wings and only the hand was bare. Ellicott takes the hands to imply human arms, and reasons that since there were four hands answering to the wings, the wings must have been attached at the shoulder. Calvin makes the hands the sign of readiness, since he who is without hands lies useless, and the wings the sign of the opposite: they signify that the angels have no motion in themselves and cannot go where they please unless divinely impelled, so that they are not borne rashly hither and thither but directed wherever God pleases. Wesley takes the power and the manner of exerting it to be secret and invisible, and the doubled phrase as confirming the certainty of the thing. Gill alone reads the whole figure of the ministers of the Gospel, taking the straight feet for walking uprightly and never turning back from the plough, and the hands on four sides for work on every side; under the wings, they show how much is done privately, where no eye sees but the eye of God. He notes that the poets gave a hundred hands to a man of business.
9:
The joined wings are described from several sides. Ellicott has the right wing of one cherub touching the left wing of the next, so that though four they constituted in some sense one creature moving by a common impulse; this holds only in motion, since when they stood the wings were let down. Wesley makes the joining hold between the two foremost and the two behind, and finds them unwearied in doing the pleasure of their Creator. Clarke turns the extended wings into a canopy level with their heads, on which the throne and the likeness of the man rested, and observes that they did not flap in flying or move like oars: as they glided in respect of their feet, so they soared in respect of their wings.

Calvin explains why going straight forward is not contradicted by the later statement that they ran like lightning and returned: they proceed in a perpetual course towards their goal without turning aside, and it does not follow that they rest when they reach it. He finds in the joined wings a lesson about providence: below there often appears dreadful confusion and the works of God seem discordant, but whoever raises his eyes to heaven sees the greatest harmony between things that look like opposites. Ellicott meets an objection, that since two wings covered their bodies a change of course would seem to require the wings to turn; the difficulty disappears if the four are arranged in a square moving as one creature, since looking every way they could always go straight forward.

On the faces, Ellicott blames the obscurity on the punctuation of the English Bible and sets them in order: the man in front as the prophet viewed them, the lion on the right, the ox on the left, the eagle behind. Clarke agrees that there was but one body to each with four faces upon it, and reports that many such compound images appear among the Asiatic idols, several now before him, with the head of a monkey or a dog on a human body, or six heads with twelve arms; all were symbolical and each had its meaning, and so had these, could we but find it out. Calvin gives the reason for four: the people were so dull that they would not acknowledge the providence of God over all the world but wished to hold him shut up in a prison, their temple being that prison, so the four faces show his providence shining over other regions. He then raises the difficulty that a later vision puts a cherub where this puts an ox, rejects as sophistry the answer that it looked like an ox at a distance and a cherub nearer, rejects the identification of cherub with ox since cherubim have not the heads of oxen, and concludes that the second vision differed here, being called the same on account of the likeness.

The last clause turns on a single word. Gill reports that the versions join it to the faces as well as the wings and render both stretched upwards, though the original has parted upwards. Ellicott rejects the rendering outright: the word never has the sense of stretched but always of separated or divided, so that the wings and the faces were separated above. Each cherub was essentially one creature, yet the four faces did not sit on one head; Calvin agrees that they are not so united that a fourfold form could be seen on one, as various forms may appear in one glass while each answers to its own original. Wesley has each face appear distinct above the shoulders, where the wings divided from one another joined the body. Gill continues his reading of the ministers of the Gospel, taking the joined wings for their concord and the upward stretch for their looking to Christ for fresh supplies of grace.
12:
What moved them is the question here, and each voice answers differently. Clarke takes the spirit for the whirlwind, so that whither it blew they went, and repeats that the motion was gliding and not progressive stepping. Ellicott takes it for one informing spirit animating all the living creatures alike, by which all their movements were ordered. Wesley takes it for the Spirit of God, whose will, command and breathing both gave and guided their motions, and cautions that going is attributed to the Spirit only by allusion, since he who is everywhere cannot properly be said to go from or to any place. Calvin settles it by the word itself: it is often put for wind and also for the human soul, but here the will or mind is meant.

Calvin also explains why the clause is repeated. Mankind can scarcely be induced to ascribe glory to the wisdom of God, being so stupid as to think he mingles all things inconsiderately, as if in the dark; and since his actions look distorted to us, the point must be pressed that these creatures are constrained to obedience, tending at once to their goal and declining to neither side. What is said of angels, he warns, ought to be referred to God himself, the intention being not to extol angelic wisdom but to set them before us as his ministers, so that we may hold that God so regulates his actions that nothing with him is distorted or uncontrolled.

The fire is described with some difficulty. Clarke has the whole substance appear to be flame, with coruscations like vibrating lamps emitting sparks such as are struck from ignited iron in a forge, and compares it to what is called warring wheels in pyrotechny, the flames seeming to conflict together. Ellicott removes a conjunction that is not in the original, so that the appearance of lamps is not a second thing but a further explanation of the first, and notes that lamps names not the material but the light, the same word being rendered elsewhere torches, firebrands or lightnings; the prophet could find no single word for his meaning and gave two, that between them the fiery brilliancy might be better conveyed. Wesley observes that the fire stood not still but, as the Hebrew has it, made itself walk up and down, and that moving itself is too much to ascribe to creatures. Calvin takes the strangeness as deliberate: something heavenly had to be mixed with the earthly figures or the vision would not have excited admiration, as the bush would not have arrested Moses had it burned and been consumed.

The running and returning closes the section. Calvin finds in the lightning an amazing swiftness, since it goes forth from one part of the world and penetrates instantly to the opposite, and reconciles the returning with the going straight forward: they do not return until they have arrived at the goal, for though many hindrances occur God breaks through them, and though the devil endeavours by his obstacles to compel God to recede, the angels go on to the end. Clarke reads the movement as circular, rapid but never increasing their distance from the spectator. Wesley has them run into the lower world to do what was to be done there and return like lightning to the upper world and the vision of God, and turns it on the reader: though we run into the affairs of this world we must not repose in them, but must presently return to God, our rest and centre. Ellicott sums up the vision so far as showing the irresistible energy of the agencies employed for the divine purposes, and their perfectly harmonious action under one supreme will, before a fresh phase opens. Gill reads throughout of the ministers of the Gospel, who have a face to go before them and work with readiness.
15:
The wheels open a second half of the vision, and Henry sets the terms: the glory of God appears not only in the splendour of his retinue above but in the steadiness of his government below, so that having seen how he does his will in the armies of heaven we may see how he does so among the inhabitants of the earth. He compares the dispensations of providence to wheels, either of a chariot in which a conqueror rides in triumph or rather of a clock, whose parts all contribute to the regular motion of the machine. Wesley works the same figure: providence orders changes, so that sometimes one spoke is uppermost and sometimes another, while the wheel turns on its axle steadily; and since the wheel stands by the living creatures, who direct its motion, all inferior creatures move as the Creator directs by the ministration of angels, visible effects being governed by invisible causes. Calvin reads them of the constant changes of the world, which may be compared to a sea, and a tempestuous one, since nothing in it is firm or calm.

Ellicott keeps the two halves together: the prophet sees this while still looking on the living creatures, and the wheel is one in the same sense that they were one and yet actually four; they had been seen in the cloud, and must now be joined below to the earth and presently above to the throne, so the wheel is upon the earth though of great height. He rejects deriving the imagery from the wheels under the bases of the temple of Solomon, since nothing in size or form corresponds, and holds it purely original. Calvin explains the delay by the magnitude of what was shown: though taken up as into heaven, the prophet could not embrace so great a vision at once, and was convicted of infirmity.

The wheel within a wheel divides them. Ellicott conceives the wheels as double, one part at right angles to the other like the equator and a meridian upon a globe, so that they could go equally well any way without turning, and grants that such a wheel would be impossible to construct, being seen only in vision. Wesley reaches the same shape, an exact sphere framed of two wheels one within the other. Clarke dissents. He allows that the right-angle reading is the usual one, but thinks the wheel within means the nave in which the spokes are inserted, and is confirmed by Chinese drawings before him in which deities walk upon wheels encompassed with fire; he adds that he has examined models built to move equally in all directions and saw that no complex wheel can do so.

The stone divides them too. Gill names the beryl and reports the Syriac rendering it chrysolite, the Arabic jasper. Ellicott denies that our beryl is meant and identifies the chrysolite of the ancients, the modern topaz, whose lustre of gold agrees with the fire and brilliant light named throughout the vision. Calvin declines to identify it at all, rejecting the rendering of Jerome that made it the colour of the sea toward Cilicia and remarking that he knows not why sea or sky took his fancy; it is enough that the stone was precious and its colour so exquisite that it drew all eyes, since God meant by the wheels to set something earthly before the prophet while raising his mind by the colour, that he might know they were no common wheels of wood. On the one likeness Calvin notes that some refer it to the living creatures, but refers it to the wheels, whose exact equality shows that in all the work of God there is the greatest arrangement, though it does not lie on the surface. Ellicott adds that the four directions stand throughout for all directions, as four winds stand for all winds.
18:
The rims are described and then measured. Clarke calls them the strakes that form the periphery, and reads the dreadfulness as sheer size, so great in diameter that it was tremendous to look from the part touching the ground to the part opposite above; Calvin agrees that the height and the terrible aspect together signify wheels so far exceeding the usual size that their magnitude was formidable, and adds that all such strangeness is meant to hold the attention of the prophet, since unless the Lord draws us violently to himself we grow torpid through sloth. Wesley has the height itself impress a fear on the beholder. Ellicott corrects the English rendering here: the wheels were both high and terrible, two characteristics, and not, as our translation seems to imply, the one the cause of the other; the height, he adds, may be inferred from the wheel standing upon the earth while the creatures beside it were seen in the cloud. Gill reports another rendering altogether, that they had fear, that is a reverence in themselves.

The eyes are read three ways. Clarke asks whether they may not be the appearance of nails holding the spokes or the bands upon the rim. Calvin takes them for a providence that never wanders, and observes that the placing is exact: had the eyes been elsewhere they would have been useless, but since the wheels turn upon their felloes, there the prophet saw them fixed; and the prophet does not say each wheel had two eyes but that they were full of eyes, which means there was not the least motion in them but was arranged and governed with the utmost reason. Ellicott takes them for the perfect knowledge God has of all his works, showing here the absolute wisdom of his doings and elsewhere the harmonious praise that results; he notes that a later chapter puts the eyes on the bodies, backs, hands and wings as well, the same vision being described now by one particular and now by another because the prophet plainly feels it impossible to describe adequately, and remarks that the Hebrew seers always looked through secondary causes to the ultimate force that originates and controls nature. Wesley takes the wheels, their motion, their height and their eyes together for the height, unsearchableness, wisdom and vigilance of divine providence.

Whether the wheels had life of their own is the last question. Clarke says plainly that they were instinct with a vital spirit and were themselves animals, and builds the whole into a chariot: four wheels, on each of which one of the compound creatures stands, the creatures forming the body of the chariot and their outspread wings the canopy, with the throne above and the appearance of a man upon it. Calvin denies them any motion of their own: the wheels rest by themselves and are set going by a higher force, so that as the living creatures move the wheels are drawn along after them. From this he draws his doctrine, that when men plan so much that they disturb the whole world, and when conspiracies are made and all things prepared for action, we should perceive that God governs everything in a secret manner surpassing our senses, and when things fall out as we think unseasonably, that angels are discharging their duty and things in themselves motionless are borne along by them. Wesley agrees, calling the wheels inferior agents and second causes which concurred with the spirit of the living creatures, so that there was a hearty accord between the superior and the inferior, an undiscerned power actuating and governing all. Calvin also notes a point of arrangement, that others join the first clause of the last verse with its second part, which he thinks too forced.
21:
Calvin presses the point that the wheels stood still. A wheel cannot stand on any part of its rim without falling to one side or rolling on, so their standing was unnatural and their moving force must have been outside themselves; and since the prophet asserts so often that their motion derives from the living creatures, it follows that all the changes seen in the world have their origin from some external source. He guards the point against being pressed too far: though the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels, the wheels comprehend nothing but only receive vigour, as the moon takes its brightness from the sun, so that they are impelled rather than endowed with the intelligence of the creatures; for God does not give mind and judgment to winter or summer, to peace or war, to calm or storm. Wesley draws the same conclusion, that the wisdom, power and counsel which guide the angels order by them all the motions of the creatures in this lower world.

The firmament is defined before it is described. Ellicott traces the word to a verb meaning to beat out, as of metals, but insists the derivative had wholly lost that reference in its use of the heavens and meant simply an expanse; the Hebrews, he adds, never appear to have entertained the classical idea of the sky as a metallic vault, the one passage that might suggest it admitting quite another explanation. He notes that the expanse is not supported by the living creatures nor resting on them, since it remained undisturbed when they let down their wings, but was simply stretched over their heads, at once separating them from the throne above and uniting them to it, so that it does for the upper part of the vision what the wheels do for the lower: they connect it with the earth, this connects it with God. Gill likewise takes it for no real firmament but the likeness of one, and gives both senses of the name, an expanse from being stretched out as a curtain and a firmament from its firmness and continuance.

Gill then turns the firmament into an argument. Since it was over the heads of the living creatures, they cannot be angels, whose habitation is in the third heaven above the firmament, and still less can they figure the three Persons, who are not under the firmament at all; they must be ministers of the Gospel, who are on earth and subject to Christ, whose throne is above it. Calvin reads the same detail the other way. The principal thing in the vision is that God was seated on his throne, for had the prophet spoken only of wheels and living creatures the vision would have been partial and inefficient; and once God is placed on his throne we understand that the angels, who inspire motion in other things, have neither vigour nor motion peculiar to themselves. The firmament is not yet the throne but a step toward it, God setting stages by which the prophet might climb according to his capacity to an immense altitude; for when we raise our eyes upward the glory of God appears nearer than on earth, and the nearer we approach him the more conspicuous his image becomes.

The crystal is left deliberately vague. Clarke describes a crystal well cut and polished with many faces, refracting the light into prismatic colours or an insufferably brilliant splendour, and reports a rendering that gives fearful ice instead, which he thinks inferior to the common translation. Ellicott denies that any particular crystal is meant, the word merely conveying some idea of the expanse beneath the throne, clear as crystal and terrible in its dazzling brightness. Wesley takes the crystal for splendour, purity and solidity together, and explains the terror as the veneration it impressed on the mind of the beholders.
23:
The wings are sorted out. Ellicott blames the excessive literalness of the English for obscuring the sense, since it seems to say that each cherub used four wings to cover his body, whereas the meaning is that each had two wings covering his body on either side, the other two being extended when they were in motion and let down at rest. Calvin removes the same obscurity by distinguishing two ways of covering, the wings that tended upwards covering the creatures themselves and their faces, and the wings joined to their bodies covering the body; he rejects as absurd the view of those who make the two sets one and the same, holding rather that the prophet is repeating what was seen before, four wings apiece, two raised upward and joined so that one creature was connected with the next. Gill agrees that two were stretched straight upward toward the firmament and joined each other. Clarke gives those upper wings a different office, making them a foundation for the firmament to rest on, which is the point Ellicott had denied when he insisted the expanse was neither supported by the creatures nor resting on them.

The sound divides them further. Clarke takes it for wind, the rustling among the wings when the whirlwind drove the wheels, like a waterfall or waters dashing against rocks, and the voice of the Almighty for distant thunder, which is how that phrase is used elsewhere. Ellicott begins with a translation point, that the same word is rendered noise three times and voice twice in this verse, and that voice should be kept throughout; and he presses each comparison in turn, thunder for the voice of the Almighty, and for the voice of speech a word that occurs elsewhere only once, where it is rendered a tumult, so that what is meant is the confused sound of a great multitude and not articulate language at all. Every comparison, he concludes, represents a sound vast and terrible but inarticulate. Wesley takes the opposite view on the one point that matters, that the prophet heard the voice in an articulate manner, though he agrees on the thunder and reads the host as a tumultuous voice of men.

Calvin makes the voice do the work of the whole passage. Precepts are expressed by the voice, this being the means of human intercourse, so that whoever bears sway proclaims by it what he wishes done; and since it had been obscure how the wheels were moved by the living creatures, the prophet now says there was a voice. He is careful not to press the figure: the wheels were not endued with ears and could not hear commands, but the prophet could not otherwise express that heaven and earth are full of angelic motion, nor that whatever happens obeys the will of God, since such obedience cannot be conceived unless a voice go before it. On the sound itself he takes the comparison from the overflow of an impetuous river, than which nothing is more terrible, a crash that seems to threaten the breaking up of things. Wesley closes the scene at rest: having done their office they present themselves before God, waiting for the commands of their Lord. Gill reads it as before of the ministers of the Gospel going out in their ministrations.
25:
A single verse turns the vision toward its close, and the voice that comes with it is placed carefully. Ellicott corrects the preposition: it came from above the firmament, not as proceeding from the firmament itself, and it is a new feature altogether, quite different from the sounds described before, and though not here expressly called articulate it is probably the same divine voice spoken of later in the book. He allows that the last clause may be no more than a repetition of the words that end the preceding verse, but prefers to read a fresh act of reverence: when the voice was heard the creatures stood still, the mighty sounds of their going were hushed and their wings fell motionless, all in an attitude of reverential attention. He then sums up the stages, the whirlwind from the north with its cloud and infolding fire as the background, the living creatures with their symbolism, the wheels joining them to the earth below, the glowing firmament joining them to the throne above, and now the throne itself and him that sat upon it. Gill takes the voice for the voice of Christ upon the throne, directing the creatures when and where to go and where to stop.

Calvin uses the same verse to guard against reading the vision as a description of God. The prophet spoke of the firmament because human minds cannot reach so great a height except by degrees, and he sets the steps in order; but what was seen was not the true heavens, nor a throne of any material substance, nor a real and natural body of a man. The prophet says so expressly, Calvin argues, lest anyone imagine that there is anything visible in God and suppose him corporeal, or gather that God can be seen by the eye, confined within place and seated like a man. One noun should have sufficed, but because we are prone to vague and erroneous opinions the prophet joins appearance to likeness, so that whatever the ancient heretics fabricated about the visible form of God is excluded by the clearest language.

Why then the form of a man at all? Calvin takes the answer from the fathers who called it a prelude to the mystery afterwards displayed to the world, that God was manifest in the flesh; and he adds that as often as God appeared under the form of man an obscure glimpse was afforded of what was at length manifested in the person of Christ. He rejects the reading of Jerome, which applies the words to the Father, since the Father was never clad in human flesh; had it merely been said that God is here represented there would have been no absurdity, for with all mention of persons removed it is true enough that the man seated on the throne was God, and the prophet himself uses the name Jehovah at the end of the chapter. He also rejects a christology then current which made the likeness a real man and the pre-existent Christ a visible God composed of uncreated elements, whose flesh was afterwards absorbed by the deity so that no trace of human nature remained, and whose body was therefore held to be everywhere and immense. Against it he sets the vision of another prophet, where the Ancient of Days wears the figure of a man on the highest summit and the Mediator is brought to him, and concludes that what is said of the likeness of a man can be transferred neither to the Father nor to the Spirit, since neither was ever manifested in flesh.
26:
Henry treats everything before this as preface. God had made himself known as Lord of angels and director of this lower world, from which it is easy to infer that whatever he promises or threatens by his prophets he is able to effect, angels being his servants and men his tools; but now that a revelation is to be given to the church we must look higher than the creatures or the wheels, to the eternal Word. He has the prophet look up at the voice as another seer afterwards did and see one like unto the Son of man, and observes that the second person sometimes tried the fashion of a man before clothing himself with it for good. From the position of the throne he draws a further point: the glory is above the firmament over their heads, so that the heads of angels themselves are under the feet of the Lord Jesus, and this dominion of the Redeemer before his incarnation magnifies his condescension.

Ellicott holds back from that identification. He fastens on the repetition of likeness and appearance, five times in this verse and four in each of the next two, and argues that the prophet labours by it to make plain that what he saw was not the realities of existing things but symbolic representations; it was not the Divine Being himself that was seen but appearances meant to impress the character of him whom no man hath seen nor can see. As with the living creatures, the form of a man was taken as the groundwork because it is the highest known in nature, and here the same basis had to be kept for want of anything better. He allows only that there may possibly be a hint of the incarnation, where Clarke states it plainly, the human form above the canopy representing him who in the fullness of time was manifested in the flesh.

The stones and colours are handled by eye. Clarke has a large well cut oriental sapphire before him, one of the most resplendent blues conceivable, and has seen the heavens assume that hue; he holds a specimen of amber to the light for a bright yellow, and reports that such was the appearance of the august Being from the reins upward, while downward he had the appearance of fire. Gill notes that the man upon the throne looked like the colour of amber. Ellicott compares a passage where the same description is given of the pavement under the feet of God rather than his throne, both indicating the clearness of the heavenly blue, renders the amber literally as an eye of bright metal, and takes the rest of the verse for an attempt by repetition to convey the brightness, with the notions of purity, power and activity that attend fire. Calvin objects to a rendering of the word that finds an angel in it, having no doubt a colour is meant; he leaves the version of Jerome doubtful but calls foolish the claim that the substance is more precious than gold and silver, since it is composed of both.

Calvin explains what the splendour did to the seer. God appeared so visible under the form of a man that the brightness dazzled his eyes; otherwise the prophet could have considered each part separately, as one looking at a man takes in his stature and the kind of his eyes. A glance distinguishes the parts of men or trees, but eyes turned on the sun are dimmed at once; and if they cannot bear the sun, how should the mind comprehend the glory of God. Wesley reads the colour as a warning: in it Christ appears against the rebellious people, he who would have visited them in the garments of salvation now putting on the garments of vengeance, the brightness round about him being his majesty, justice and unstained holiness.
28:
The bow is the last thing seen and the point on which the voices divide. Gill describes it plainly as the reflection of the rays of the sun in a thin watery cloud. Clarke has it stretched over the canopy with all its colours vivid and in perfection, red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet, and insists that every metal and colour in the vision is to be understood at its utmost perfection of shape and splendour, while still being only the appearance of the likeness, a faint representation of the real thing. Ellicott makes the phrase in the day of rain do real work, taking it as no mere reference to a natural phenomenon but a deliberate link with the promise made after the flood, showing that the God who has presented his attributes of terrible majesty will add those of mercy and loving-kindness, since it was in both alike that he was to be made known through the prophet now receiving his commission. Wesley reads it the same way, that mercy and truth, both according to covenant, are about the throne. Clarke draws the same comfort for the history: though there should be destruction and sore tribulation, the token of the covenant shows there should not be total ruin, and after a long captivity they should be restored.

Calvin refuses the reading. He grants it is plausible, and that this is how the corresponding vision of a throne surrounded by a bow is usually taken, as showing God reconciled; but the opinion that the bow here is a testimony of favour does not seem to him proved, since the whole vision is opposed to it. On the bow itself he is expansive. Profane men call it the bow of Juno and imagine she performs the commands of the gods, whereas Scripture calls it the bow of God, and not, as many falsely suppose, because it was created after the flood; those who take the promise to mean the bow did not exist before distort it. God rather inscribed a testimony of his favour on a thing by no means in accordance with it, freely using his creatures as he wills; for the bow is often a sign of continued rain and seems as if it attracted the shower, so that its very aspect may cause terror, and against that fear God set the assurance that as often as it appears the earth is determined safe from a deluge.

The chapter closes with the prophet on his face, which Wesley reads as deep humility and reverence and Ellicott as the ordinary effect of an immediate manifestation of the Divine, always overpowering to man; Wesley adds that what was shown was not the full glory of God but such as the prophet might bear. Ellicott ends by setting the vision in the life of the prophet, noting that he saw it four times: here at his call; shortly afterwards when he is sent to denounce judgment and foretell the destruction of the city and the temple; a year and a half later, when he is made to understand the abominations wrought in the temple while it still stood, until the glory of the Lord forsakes the house and departs from the city; and finally in the prophecy of restoration, when that same presence re-enters and fills the house. Clarke declines to interpret at all beyond a guess. He has tried to give the forms, positions and colours correctly, but asks who can explain their meaning, and doubts whether conjectures already abundant should be multiplied; his own inclination is that the whole points to the state of the people about to be subdued and carried away, the creatures, wheels, fires and whirlwinds standing emblematically for the sword, fire, pestilence and famine employed in their destruction, with God appearing throughout to show that the conqueror is only his instrument.
